sections.title: Meet and identify
sections.description: Greet people, exchange basic personal details, use numbers, and follow simple classroom instructions.

units.title: Hello!
units.canDo: Greet people, say goodbye, and say who you are

tip.title: German has different forms of ‘you’
tip.body:
Use **ich bin** for “I am” and **du bist** with one person you know well. German changes the form of **sein** to match the subject; English usually changes only “am/is/are.”

Use capitalised **Sie sind** in formal situations. **Sie** takes the same verb form as plural “they,” but the capital letter shows the polite meaning. With **heißen**, German literally says that someone “is called” a name.

units.title: Where are you from?
units.canDo: Ask and answer questions about names, origins, and where people live

tip.title: Put the question word first
tip.body:
German W-questions begin with a question word, then the conjugated verb: **Wo wohnst du?** English needs “do” in many questions, but German does not.

Use **wo** for location and **woher** for origin. An answer about origin uses **aus**; an answer about where someone lives normally uses **in**.

sourceAccept: What is the name of the city?
What's the name of the city?
The name of the city is Berlin.

units.title: Spell it, please
units.canDo: Spell a name and ask someone to repeat or speak slowly

tip.title: A polite instruction keeps Sie after the verb
tip.body:
For a polite instruction, use the verb form that goes with **Sie**, put it first, and keep **Sie** directly after it: **Sprechen Sie langsam.** English usually uses only the base verb and leaves out “you.”

**Bitte** can come at the beginning or later in the instruction. **Wie bitte?** is a useful fixed question when you did not hear or understand something.

sourceAccept: Please say it once more, slowly.
Please say it one more time, slowly.

units.title: Numbers and age
units.canDo: Give your age, a number, and simple quantities

tip.title: Age uses sein, but possession uses haben
tip.body:
German asks **Wie alt bist du?** and answers **Ich bin zwanzig.** This matches English “I am twenty,” but German does not need a word for “years” in the short answer.

Use **haben** for things you have: **ich habe**, **du hast**, and **Sie haben**. The question **wie viel?** asks “how much?” or “how many?” when the noun is understood.

sentences.target: Wie viel ist zehn plus zehn?
sourceAccept: How much is ten plus ten?

units.title: In the classroom
units.canDo: Follow simple classroom instructions and check an answer

tip.title: Formal instructions start with the verb
tip.body:
A polite German instruction starts with the verb and then uses **Sie**: **Lesen Sie die Frage.** English also starts with the verb, but normally leaves “you” unspoken.

The verb keeps the same ending as in a statement with formal **Sie**. **Bitte** can soften the instruction, and it can appear before or after the main instruction.

sentences.target: Lesen Sie die Antwort noch einmal.
sourceAccept: Read the answer one more time.

sections.title: People and everyday things
sections.description: Talk about family, identify everyday objects, discuss food and drink, describe simple actions, and correct basic information.

units.title: My family
units.canDo: Identify close family members and say who belongs to whom

tip.title: Possessives match the family noun
tip.body:
German **mein** and **dein** change before some nouns. Use **mein Vater** and **mein Kind**, but **meine Mutter** and **meine Eltern**. English “my” and “your” never change this way.

Use **er** for a male person and **sie** for a female person. Do not confuse lowercase **sie** (“she”) with capitalised **Sie** (“you” in formal situations).

sourceAccept: My parents are married to each other.
The child is ten years old.
The kid is ten years old.

units.title: What is that?
units.canDo: Name common objects and recognise their grammatical gender

tip.title: Learn the article with every noun
tip.body:
German has three words for “the”: **der**, **die**, and **das**. The article belongs with the noun, so learn **der Tisch**, **die Tasche**, and **das Buch** as complete units. English uses “the” for all three.

For “a,” use **ein** with masculine and neuter nouns, but **eine** with feminine nouns. German plurals also vary, so learn the plural together with each new noun.

units.title: Food I like
units.canDo: Name basic food and drink and say what you enjoy

tip.title: Use gern for things you like doing
tip.body:
German often expresses “like” with **gern** plus an action: **Ich trinke gern Tee** literally means “I drink tea gladly.” Unlike English, German does not need a separate verb meaning “like” here.

For a yes-or-no question, move the conjugated verb to the front: **Trinkst du gern Kaffee?** A food or drink can also be the subject with **schmecken**: **Der Käse schmeckt.**

sourceAccept: Do you like to eat cheese?
Do you like to drink coffee?
Do you like to eat cheese?

sentences.source: Do the bread and cheese taste good?
sourceAccept: Are the bread and cheese tasty?

units.title: Things we do
units.canDo: Describe simple present actions for different people

tip.title: The verb ending shows who acts
tip.body:
For most German verbs, remove **-en** and add an ending: **ich lerne**, **du lernst**, **er lernt**, **wir lernen**, **ihr lernt**, and **Sie lernen**. English changes far less, so the German subject and ending must agree.

In a basic statement, put the conjugated verb after the subject. In a yes-or-no question, put it first: **Arbeitet ihr heute?**

units.title: No, not, none
units.canDo: Deny, contrast, and correct simple information

tip.title: Use nicht for actions and kein for nouns
tip.body:
Use **nicht** to negate an action or description: **Ich arbeite nicht** and **Das ist nicht richtig**. English usually uses “not” with an auxiliary verb, but German can place **nicht** later in the clause.

Use **kein** before a masculine or neuter noun and **keine** before a feminine or plural noun: **kein Kaffee**, **kein Wasser**, but **keine Milch**. These combine the ideas of English “not a” or “no.”

sourceAccept: I do not have any water.

sentences.source: No, I do not drink water.
sourceAccept: No, I am not drinking water.

sentences.target: Die Antwort ist leider falsch, aber die Nummer ist richtig.
sentences.source: Unfortunately, the answer is wrong, but the number is correct.
sourceAccept: Sadly, the answer is wrong, but the number is correct.
Unfortunately, the answer is incorrect, but the number is right.

sentences.source: Unfortunately, I do not have a number.
sourceAccept: Unfortunately, I don't have a number.
Sadly, I do not have a number.
Sadly, I don't have a number.

sections.title: Routines and direct objects
sections.description: Describe daily routines, ask for everyday items, order in a café, talk about a home, and make simple plans.

units.title: My day
units.canDo: Describe a basic daily routine and say when things happen

tip.title: The conjugated verb stays in position two
tip.body:
A German statement keeps its conjugated verb in the second position. You can begin with the person: **Ich frühstücke morgens.** If you begin with the time, the person moves after the verb: **Morgens frühstücke ich.** English normally keeps the subject before the verb in both versions.

Some common routine verbs change their stem: **du fährst** and **du liest**. Learn **ich stehe auf** as a useful routine chunk for “I get up”; the small word **auf** goes at the end here.

units.title: I need a…
units.canDo: Ask for, find, and buy common everyday items

tip.title: Masculine objects change to den or einen
tip.body:
A direct object receives the action. For a masculine noun, **der** changes to **den**, and **ein** changes to **einen**: **der Apfel**, but **Ich nehme den Apfel** or **Ich suche einen Apfel**. English articles do not change this way.

Feminine and neuter articles stay the same in the accusative: **die Banane**, **Ich nehme die Banane**; **das Ticket**, **Ich brauche das Ticket**.

sentences.source: I am looking for the apple.

sourceAccept: I am searching for a table.

units.title: At the café
units.canDo: Order breakfast, ask the price, and pay politely

tip.title: Ich möchte makes a polite order
tip.body:
Use **ich möchte** for a polite request: **Ich möchte einen Kaffee.** It is much closer to English “I would like” than a direct **Ich will**. With informal **du**, ask **Möchtest du ...?**; with formal **Sie**, ask **Möchten Sie ...?**

The item ordered is a direct object, so masculine **ein** becomes **einen**. To ask a price, use **Was kostet ...?** for one item and **Was kosten ...?** for more than one.

sentences.source: I would like to order breakfast.

sentences.target: Möchten Sie Kaffee oder Tee bestellen?
sentences.source: Would you like to order coffee or tea?
targetAccept: Möchtest du Kaffee oder Tee bestellen?
Möchtet ihr Kaffee oder Tee bestellen?

sourceAccept: How much does the coffee cost?

units.title: My home
units.canDo: Describe rooms, furniture, and where things are in a home

tip.title: Use es gibt for there is and there are
tip.body:
German uses **es gibt** for both English “there is” and “there are”: **Es gibt ein Bad** and **Es gibt zwei Zimmer**. The thing that exists is a direct object, so a masculine noun uses **einen**: **Es gibt einen Schrank.**

Use **hier** for “here” and **dort** for “there.” They can begin the sentence, but the conjugated verb still comes second: **Hier ist die Küche.**

sentences.target: Das Bett ist klein, aber der Schrank ist groß.
sentences.source: The bed is small, but the cupboard is big.
sourceAccept: The bed is small, but the cupboard is large.
The bed is small, but the wardrobe is big.
The bed is small, but the cabinet is big.

sentences.source: The kitchen is there and the bathroom is here.

sentences.target: Es gibt ein Bad und eine Küche.

sourceAccept: There's a bathroom and a kitchen.

units.title: People and plans review
units.canDo: Exchange a short profile and talk about who meets or visits whom

tip.title: Wer asks who; wen asks whom
tip.body:
Use **wer** when the unknown person does the action: **Wer besucht den Freund?** Use **wen** when the unknown person receives the action: **Wen besucht die Freundin?** English often uses “who” for both, so German makes the contrast more visible.

The same contrast appears in articles. A masculine subject uses **der**, while a masculine direct object uses **den**: **Der Freund besucht die Freundin. Die Freundin besucht den Freund.**

sections.title: Around town
sections.description: Find places, use public transport, follow directions, talk about abilities, and arrange appointments.

units.title: Places nearby
units.canDo: Ask where public places are and understand simple location directions

tip.title: Ask wo for a fixed location
tip.body:
Use **wo** when you want to know where a place is. German puts the conjugated verb directly after the question word: **Wo ist die Post?** English adds “is” in the same kind of question, but does not use “do.”

For a short route answer, **links**, **rechts**, and **geradeaus** can stand alone. To describe distance, use **nahe** with **sein**: **Die Bank ist nahe.**

sentences.source: The hotel is on the left.

units.title: Getting around
units.canDo: Say when transport leaves and arrives and where to get on or off

tip.title: Separable prefixes move to the end
tip.body:
In a main clause, German splits verbs such as **abfahren** and **ankommen**. The conjugated verb takes position 2, while the prefix moves to the end: **Der Zug fährt ab.** English keeps “leave” as one piece.

The same pattern appears in questions: **Wann kommt der Bus an?** Keep the prefix at the end even when a time word begins the sentence: **Jetzt steigt sie ein.**

The train is departing on time.

units.title: Which way?

tip.title: Use short commands for directions
tip.body:
Formal German directions often use the verb first with **Sie**: **Gehen Sie geradeaus.** English directions usually omit “you,” but German keeps polite **Sie**. In everyday signs or quick instructions, you may also hear the infinitive alone.

Use **zu** for a destination such as a place: **zum Bahnhof** and **zur Bank**. Use **nach** before a city or a direction without an article: **nach Berlin**, **nach links**.

units.title: I can do that
units.canDo: Talk about abilities and ask simple questions about permission

tip.title: Put the second verb at the end
tip.body:
The modal verb **können** changes to match the subject and takes position 2. The action stays as an infinitive at the end: **Ich kann schwimmen.** English puts “can” before the action too, but German sends the action to the clause end.

In a question, the modal comes first: **Kann ich hier parken?** For one person, use **kannst du**; for several people, **könnt ihr**; and formally, **können Sie**.

sourceAccept: We are able to dance together.

sourceAccept: Am I allowed to park here?

units.title: Appointments
units.canDo: Arrange a simple appointment and say what you want or need to do

tip.title: Time first still means verb second
tip.body:
Like **können**, the modals **wollen** and **müssen** send the action infinitive to the end: **Ich will anfangen.** and **Wir müssen gehen.** English keeps the action beside “want to” or “must,” but German separates them.

A time phrase can come first for emphasis. The conjugated verb must still be the second element, so the subject follows it: **Am Montag will ich anfangen.** Use **am** with days and **um** with clock times.

sections.title: Describe life
sections.description: Talk about the weather, your clothes, how you feel, your free time, and what you did yesterday.

units.title: Weather today
units.canDo: understand a basic weather report

tip.title: Talking about the weather
tip.body:
In German, to talk about the weather, we use **es** (it) just like in English. We can say **es regnet** (it is raining) or **es ist kalt** (it is cold). 

Remember that the verb always stays in the second position in a statement, so if you start with **heute** (today), the verb comes next, followed by **es** or the subject.

sentences.source: It is raining and the wind is cold.
sourceAccept: It's raining and the wind is cold.
It rains and the wind is cold.

tip.title: Pointing things out with dieser
tip.body:
When pointing something out, use **dieser** (this) instead of the normal article **der**. 

The ending changes to match the gender of the noun you are pointing at: **dieser Schuh** (der), **diese Jacke** (die), **dieses Hemd** (das). For plural words, also use **diese**.

tip.title: Mir geht es...
tip.body:
To say how you are doing, Germans literally say "it goes to me...". The word **mir** means "to me".

If you want to say you feel well, say **mir geht es gut** or **es geht mir gut**.

tip.title: Gern vs Lieber
tip.body:
We learned that adding **gern** after a verb means you like doing that activity.

To say you prefer an activity, use the word **lieber** (rather) instead. Just like **gern**, it usually goes right after the verb.

sourceAccept: I like to listen to music.

sourceAccept: We are going to the movie theater.

units.title: Yesterday, briefly
units.canDo: understand a few common past statements

tip.title: Talking about the past
tip.body:
To talk about the past, German uses a helping verb (usually **haben**) in the second position of the sentence.

The real action goes to the very end of the sentence and usually starts with **ge-** (like **gemacht** or **gekauft**).

If the action involves moving from A to B (like travelling or coming), use **sein** (to be) as the helping verb instead of **haben**.

sentences.target: Ich bin gestern in Berlin gewesen.
targetAccept: Gestern bin ich in Berlin gewesen.
sourceAccept: I have been in Berlin yesterday.

sentences.target: Hast du das Buch schon gekauft?

tip.title: Who is it for?
tip.body:
When you use **für** (for), the next word is the direct object (accusative). So masculine words change their article to **den** or **einen**.

Feminine and neuter words don't change. You can say **für das Einzelzimmer** or **für den Vater**.

tip.title: Where are you heading?
tip.body:
When you want to know the destination, use **wohin** (where to). Compare it with **wo** (where), which asks for a fixed location.

Use **hin** for a journey there, and **zurück** for the journey back.

tip.title: Adding some flavor
tip.body:
The word **denn** often doesn't translate directly. In questions, it makes you sound friendlier or more curious, a bit like "so" or "tell me" in English.

Separable verbs like **einladen** split in simple sentences. The **ein** goes right to the end!

tip.title: Capitalizing on nouns
tip.body:
In German, every single noun starts with a capital letter. Not just names like Leon, but words like **Vorname** (first name) and **Land** (country).

This makes it very easy to spot the important words when you're filling out a form or reading a message!

tip.title: First this, then that
tip.body:
When you put a time word like **zuerst** (first) or **dann** (then) at the start of your sentence, the verb must stay in position two.

That means the person doing the action moves to position three, directly after the verb!
